title: Rate-smoothing kernel-aware queue manager for continuous batching
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Our continuous-batching pipeline shows recurring p95/p99 latency spikes when short inputs collide with long-sequence prefill/decodes and trigger non-optimal kernels. Existing admission heuristics are brittle under bursty arrivals and heterogeneous sequence-length distributions. This ticket designs and implements a rate-smoothing queue manager that tightly couples admission control with kernel-aware batch shaping to reduce tail latency while preserving throughput and GPU utilization.

Goals:
- Reduce p95 latency for mixed workloads by >= 20% without regressing median throughput.
- Avoid unnecessary kernel-switch churn by predicting kernel budget before admission.
- Provide safe fallbacks that maintain latency SLOs under sudden bursts.
- Expose config flags for tenant-level trade-offs (latency vs cost).

Design summary:
1) Rate-smoothing window: introduce a sliding-window token budget per GPU (configurable window ms) that smooths admission rates instead of flat token buckets. The window uses a decaying moving average of admitted token costs (seq_len * tokens) to avoid admitting large prefill bursts that saturate kernel budgets.
2) Kernel-aware admission: before admitting a prefill, estimate kernel footprint from profile histograms (sequence length distribution + model variant). If projected kernel-switch or memory budget would exceed a kernel-change threshold, gate admission and either queue for the next shaped batch or route to a compatible fast-path model variant.
3) Batch-shaping heuristics: compile admitted requests into a shaped batch using a small dynamic programming heuristic that prioritizes grouping similar sequence lengths and attention modes to minimize kernel switching cost. For large variance inputs, create a short-hold window (5-15ms) to let a few similar-length requests accumulate.
4) Tail-latency mitigations: introduce admission preemption for very old requests (age-based boost), and an emergency drain that triggers a low-latency decode-only kernel when p95 exceeds threshold.
5) Telemetry & knobs: per-tenant window size, kernel-switch sensitivity, age-boost weight, and fallback model mapping. Emit new metrics: admitted_token_rate_smoothed, kernel_switch_count, shaped_batch_variance, emergency_drain_count.

Trade-offs and considerations:
- Waiting to shape batches can increase median latency for the few requests that wait but reduces p95 for the overall service. We expose tenant knobs so teams can tune for PLG vs enterprise latency needs.
- Heuristic complexity vs CPU overhead: the DP-based batch shaper runs in O(n*L) for small n (batch cap) and is optimized for fast returns; we will gate expensive path by request rate thresholds.
- Kernel footprint estimation relies on up-to-date histograms; we will seed from recent runtime telemetry and add periodic offline recalibration job.

Acceptance criteria:
- Bench: p95 reduction >= 20% on mixed workload simulation (40% short, 40% medium, 20% long seqs) with <5% throughput regression. Link to bench dashboard must show results.
- Feature flags: all behavior behind runtime flags for canary rollout.
- Observability: new metrics emitted and dashboard created; alert runbook for emergency_drain > 0.
- Integration: compatible with existing prefill throttler and backpressure signals; no regressions in stability tests.

Implementation plan (high level):
- Week 1: implement sliding-window token budget + simple kernel estimate and unit tests.
- Week 2: add batch-shaper heuristic + integration tests and offline simulation harness.
- Week 3: benching across instance types, add telemetry, iterate on thresholds.
- Week 4: canary in runtime-1.20 on 10% traffic, measure, roll to prod.
